name: Volkswagen Beetle
assembly: Osnabrück, Germany (Karmann — convertibles only, not the coupe)
Puebla, Mexico (the last plant standing; built the final car in 2003)

length.sourceNote: Infobox range 4,079-4,140 mm across the model's trims and years, not attributed to a specific one; recorded here as the shorter figure per project convention. NHTSA's Canadian Vehicle Specifications independently gives a dated 4,140 mm for a 1974 'Beetle' and 4,190 mm for the 1974 'Super Beetle' — both consistent with this range (see the '1200' and '1302S' trims).

width.sourceNote: Infobox range 1,539-1,585 mm, not attributed to a specific trim or year; recorded here as the narrower figure per project convention.

height.sourceNote: The infobox gives a single figure, not a range, for the whole model line.

wheelbase.sourceNote: Infobox range 2,400-2,420 mm, recorded here as the shorter figure. The 20 mm difference is the 1970 Super Beetle's longer front end, described in the article body as a 2 cm wheelbase increase, and confirmed by NHTSA's Canadian Vehicle Specifications (2,400 mm 'Beetle' vs 2,420 mm 'Super Beetle', both 1974) — see the '1302S' trim.

kerbWeight.sourceNote: Infobox range 730-930 kg, unattributed to a specific trim, year or market. NHTSA's Canadian Vehicle Specifications gives dated, per-variant figures inside this range for 1974: 860 kg for the 'Beetle' and 920 kg for the 'Super Beetle' (recorded on the matching trims below). Dutch RDW vehicle-registration data for several individually plated 1200-badged cars puts the kerb weight at 770-790 kg, which is lower than the Canadian figure for the same nameplate — plausibly a lighter market specification rather than a contradiction, but registration records are for individual cars, not a manufacturer spec, so it is not used as a structured figure here.

displacement.sourceNote: The Type 122 engine introduced in 1954, bore enlarged to 77 mm, replacing the original 1938-1954 1131 cc unit.

power.sourceNote: Published directly in kW for the 1965 '1200A', the badge given to the standard model once numeric designations replaced 'Standard'/'Export'. It is the same Type 122 1192 cc engine introduced in 1954, described there as 30 PS (a 5 PS increase over its 1131 cc predecessor) — 30 PS at 1 PS = 0.73549875 kW is 22.1 kW, consistent with the figure recorded here.

mass.sourceNote: NHTSA Canadian Vehicle Specifications, 1974 model year 'Beetle' record — a dated Canadian-market curb weight inside Wikipedia's unattributed 730-930 kg range for the whole model line.

dragCoefficient.sourceNote: Listed there for the 'Volkswagen Beetle (original design)', dated 1938; the main Beetle article states the same 0.48 figure without a date qualifier. Recorded here on the earliest trim in this batch (from 1954) because the body shape changed only incrementally — larger glass in 1965, a reshaped nose on the 1970 Super Beetle — so applying one figure across the range is reasonable but is not itself sourced per trim.

frontalArea.sourceNote: Derived, not published: the site's standing 0.85 x width x height approximation, using this trim's CVS-sourced width and height (1,550 x 1,500 mm). No drag-area (CdA) figure exists for the Beetle on Wikipedia's drag-coefficients list to check this estimate against.

displacement.sourceNote: Introduced August 1965, using the longer-stroke crankshaft (64 mm to 69 mm) from the Volkswagen Type 3.

power.sourceNote: 40 PS (DIN) at introduction in August 1965, converted at 1 PS = 0.73549875 kW. Uprated to 44 PS (32.4 kW) in 1971 — the same output the article gives for the contemporary 1302 — but no exact date or intermediate figure is given for the 1300 lineage itself, so only the 1965 introductory figure is recorded here.

displacement.sourceNote: Introduced September 1967 alongside the three-speed semi-automatic transmission.

power.sourceNote: Published directly in kW. Discontinued in 1970 when the 1302 range took over as the larger-engined Beetle.

displacement.sourceNote: The more powerful of the two engines introduced with the August 1970 1302 range; the base 1302 kept the 1300's 1,285 cc unit at 44 PS (32.4 kW).

power.sourceNote: 50 PS (DIN), converted at 1 PS = 0.73549875 kW. Autocar magazine called the 14% power increase over the base 1302 'very modest for the size of the engine'. Superseded by the curved-windscreen 1303 range in August 1972.

mass.sourceNote: NHTSA Canadian Vehicle Specifications, 1974 model year 'Super Beetle' record.

wheelbase.sourceNote: 20 mm longer than the standard 1200/1300's 2,400 mm, matching the article's own description of a 2 cm wheelbase increase for the Super Beetle's MacPherson-strut front end.

frontalArea.sourceNote: Derived, not published: the site's standing 0.85 x width x height approximation, using this trim's CVS-sourced width and height (1,570 x 1,500 mm).

displacement.sourceNote: The same 1,584 cc displacement carried since 1970, now with a Bosch Digifant fuel-injection system, catalytic converter, lambda probe and electric ignition, standardised from late 1992 for the 1993 model year — built in Puebla, Mexico, the only plant still making the car. No power figure is published for this final, catalysed state of tune.

hero.alt: Cream-coloured Volkswagen Beetle photographed from the front three-quarter angle in a grassy setting, showing the rounded wings, split chrome bumper overriders and a German number plate
hero.caption: A 1965-1966 Käfer — the model year the larger, curved windows arrived, the single biggest visual change the shape ever received.

gallery.alt: Pale green Volkswagen Beetle photographed from the rear three-quarter angle, showing the oval rear window, twin engine-lid air vents and a Belgian number plate
gallery.caption: The oval rear window used before the 1958 change to a larger rectangular one — one of the easiest ways to date an early car at a glance.

gallery.alt: Overhead colour photograph of the Wolfsburg assembly line, with dozens of Beetle bodies in various colours moving along overhead conveyor tracks and workers fitting components
gallery.caption: Wolfsburg at the plant's peak: annual production passed 1.6 million cars by 1965, averaging 6,800 a day.

gallery.alt: Cream Volkswagen Beetle with a racing number 53 in a white circle and a red-white-blue centre stripe, styled as the Disney character Herbie
gallery.caption: Herbie, Disney's sentient Beetle, starred in a five-decade run of films from 1968 onward and is credited with helping sales in the late 1960s and early 1970s.
